opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it's going to change things quite a lot, though maybe not in the way people first imagine.

When people hear "AI for theory," they often picture a model that just proves the big open conjecture for you. That may happen someday, but the more immediate change is in the texture of daily research. So much of a theorist's time goes into things that aren't the core creative idea. You're checking whether a lemma you vaguely remember is actually true. You're digging through papers to find whether someone has already done the case you care about. You're working out a tedious calculation, or trying ten variants of a construction to see which one doesn't immediately break. Reasoning models are getting genuinely good at that layer. They can act like a tireless collaborator who's read a huge amount of literature and is happy to grind through the details.

What that does, I think, is let you explore much more. In complexity theory, for example, you often have a hunch: maybe this technique from circuit lower bounds could say something about this derandomization question. Before, testing that hunch could cost you a week or two. If a model can quickly sketch whether the idea is plausible, or point out the obvious obstacle, you can try many more directions. Research becomes less about committing to one path and more about rapidly searching a space of ideas.

There's also the verification side. Theorists care a lot about correctness, and proofs are long and subtle. Having a model, ideally combined with formal tools, that reads your argument skeptically and says "step three doesn't follow" is incredibly valuable. It won't replace peer review, but it can catch a lot earlier.

That said, I don't think the human role disappears. If anything, it shifts toward taste: deciding which questions matter, which definitions are the right ones, what a result actually means. A lot of the deepest progress in theory came from someone reframing a problem, finding the right abstraction, rather than just solving a fixed problem. That's still something humans are very much driving, at least for now.

So my short answer: in the near term, reasoning models make theorists much more productive and adventurous. Longer term, I honestly think they'll become real collaborators, contributing ideas, not just checking them. And I find that exciting rather than threatening, because the goal of theory was always to understand things, and more understanding, from wherever it comes, is a good thing.

r001.rationale: The response says a hunch that might take a researcher a week or two to test can be assessed quickly by a model, conveying that some human-difficult research work may be easy for AI.

r002.rationale: It predicts that AI may eventually contribute ideas, but does not say researchers can make discoveries by digesting ideas generated by AI.

r003.rationale: It discusses theory and gives a complexity theory example, but does not predict benefits beyond mathematics or explain that AI reasoning is general.

r004.rationale: It describes models as productive collaborators, but does not envision universal access to top-level reasoning ability through AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it's already changing it, and faster than most of us in the theory community expected a couple of years ago.

Let me separate a few things. The first is the mundane but real part: reasoning models are becoming very good at the kind of work that used to eat up a lot of a theorist's week. Checking whether a lemma is actually true, finding the counterexample you half-suspected existed, recalling that some result from a 1990s paper already does what you need, or doing the tedious case analysis that nobody wants to write out. That alone is a big shift. A lot of what we call "research taste" is really about knowing which directions are worth spending a month on, and if you can get a reliable signal in an afternoon instead of a month, you explore many more directions. I think the throughput of trying ideas goes up a lot.

The second part is more interesting and more uncertain. In complexity theory, the kind of problems I work on, the hard part is rarely the verification. It's coming up with the right question, the right intermediate object, the right notion of "hardness" that makes a proof go through. Right now the models are quite strong when the problem is well-posed and there's a clear target. They're less strong at the thing where you stare at a question for a year and realize it was the wrong question. But I don't think that gap is permanent. We've seen models go from not being able to do olympiad problems to doing them at a very high level, and the distance from there to "open but tractable" research problems is smaller than people think.

So what does the researcher's job become? I suspect it shifts toward problem selection, toward understanding what's actually important, and toward judging whether a proposed proof is not just correct but illuminating. Correctness is going to get cheap. Insight, meaning the kind of proof that tells you why something is true and opens up ten follow-up questions, is still the thing we value, and it's worth asking whether models will produce that or whether we'll still be the ones curating it.

I'll also say something a bit personal. Part of why I became a theorist is that I like the feeling of understanding something deeply, and I don't think that goes away just because a model can also do it. Mathematicians still prove things that computers can verify. But the social structure of the field, who gets credit, what counts as a contribution, how we train students, is going to have to adapt. If a PhD student's first year used to be learning to grind through technical arguments, and now that's cheap, we need to think hard about what the new first year looks like.

And finally, there's a feedback loop I find exciting. Theoretical computer science has a lot to say about these systems, about what they can and can't compute efficiently, about learning, about verification. So it's not just that AI changes theory work. Theory might be one of the fields that helps us understand what these reasoning models are actually doing. I'd like to be on both sides of that.

r001.rationale: The response says models can quickly check lemmas, find counterexamples, and handle case analysis that used to consume researchers’ time, making some formerly difficult work much easier for AI.

r002.rationale: It discusses exploring more directions and researchers’ role in selecting problems, but does not say researchers can digest ideas generated by AI to produce new discoveries.

r003.rationale: The response focuses on theoretical computer science and mentions olympiad problems, but does not predict benefits beyond mathematics or explain that the models’ reasoning is general.

r004.rationale: It does not envision universal access to top-level reasoning ability through AI.

astra-6.text:
I think they could change both how we solve problems and which problems we choose to work on. A lot of theoretical research involves trying an idea, working through the details, discovering where it fails, and then trying something else. A reasoning model could help with that process—checking an argument, exploring a small example, or suggesting a different approach. That could make it much faster to get useful feedback on an intuition.

But there’s a big difference between an argument that sounds convincing and a proof that is actually correct. Sometimes the entire difficulty of a problem is hidden in one step that looks innocuous. So we need to be able to scrutinize the model’s reasoning, and ideally verify parts of it formally.

What I find particularly interesting is whether these models can eventually help us discover new concepts. In theoretical research, progress isn’t always about solving a problem as stated. Sometimes it’s about finding the right definition or asking a better question. If AI can participate in that process, then it could become a much deeper collaborator. I’m optimistic about that possibility, but I think we should distinguish it from simply getting better at answering existing questions.

r002.rationale: It mentions AI suggesting approaches and potentially helping researchers discover concepts, but does not say researchers can develop new discoveries by digesting ideas generated by AI.

r003.rationale: The response discusses theoretical research generally, but does not predict benefits beyond mathematics or attribute them to general reasoning capabilities.

r004.rationale: It does not describe universal access to top-level reasoning ability through AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’ll change how we spend our time. In theoretical research, you often have an idea, and then you spend a long time checking whether it works: trying examples, looking for counterexamples, working through technical details. Reasoning models could help with that process. You might explore more directions because the cost of testing an idea becomes much lower.

But there’s a distinction between producing a plausible argument and proving something. A very small gap can invalidate a proof, so verification remains essential. Ideally, models would help produce arguments that we can check carefully, perhaps with formal proof tools.

The possibility I find most exciting is that they become collaborators that suggest connections we wouldn’t have considered. Then the researcher’s work may shift toward choosing questions, recognizing which ideas are meaningful, and understanding why a result is true. And, of course, these capabilities are developing, so I’m uncertain how far that shift will go.
